title: Hydrogen storage properties of AZ31–carbon black composite: the role of Ni and Ti catalysts at different reaction temperatures
abstract: Abstract High-energy ball milling was used to create AZ31 composites modified with carbon black (CB), nickel (Ni), and titanium (Ti) in order to address the slow sorption kinetics of magnesium-based hydrogen storage materials. The effect of additive type and concentration on microstructural evolution and kinetic mechanisms was examined in a systematic investigation of the hydrogen storage performance over a temperature range of 375, 350, and 325 °C. Kinetic modeling using the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) and Arrhenius equations revealed a quantitative mechanistic dichotomy between the additives. Nickel acts as a potent "surface kinetic accelerator," driving ultra-fast hydrogen dissociation via surface spillover. This mechanism significantly lowered the apparent activation energy (Ea ≈ 141.3 kJ/mol), enabling the AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni composite to achieve 95% hydrogen saturation in just 702 s at 375 °C and maintain rapid kinetics (1040 s) at 325 °C. Conversely, titanium functions as a "bulk structural modifier." Although Ti agglomeration shifted the rate-limiting step toward bulk lattice diffusion (elevating Ea to 182.0 kJ/mol), it provided robust Zener pinning and deep nucleation pathways. Consequently, while Ni excels in reaction velocity, the AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti composite successfully prevents high-temperature grain coarsening, achieving an exceptional maximum reversible capacity of 4.00 wt% even at the lowest operating temperature of 325 °C (outperforming the 3.65 wt% of the Ni-doped composite). This study highlights a targeted design strategy that balances ultra-fast kinetics with thermodynamic microstructural stability.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Hydrogen offers a viable solution for future energy systems, yet its practical deployment hinges on the development of efficient storage technologies. Compared to high-pressure gas and cryogenic liquids, solid-state storage using metal hydrides provides superior safety and volumetric density [ 1 ,  2 ]. Among the available candidates, magnesium (Mg) stands out for its high gravimetric capacity (7.6 wt%), abundance, and low cost [ 3 ]. However, the commercial application of Mg-based hydrides is severely restricted by sluggish sorption kinetics and high thermodynamic stability, which typically necessitate operating temperatures above 300 °C [ 4 ].

To overcome these constraints, methodologies such as nanostructuring through high-energy ball milling (HEBM) and catalytic doping have been extensively implemented [ 5 ]. HEBM successfully creates lattice defects and makes diffusion distances shorter. Transition metal catalysts, on the other hand, make it easier for hydrogen to break down. While pure magnesium is still the main focus of basic research, the commercial AZ31 alloy is a better starting point because it is easy to find and has well-known processing methods. Alloying elements such as Al and Zn slightly lower the theoretical capacity, but they are known to change the thermodynamic pathways and make cycling stability better [ 6 ].

Despite these advances, there remains a critical research gap in systematically understanding the synergistic effects of co-adding carbonaceous materials and structurally distinct transition metals onto a commercial AZ31 alloy matrix. Previous studies often view carbon merely as a lubricant or a simple process control agent, while transition metals are broadly categorized as general catalysts without differentiating their specific structural roles. To address this void, this study articulates a testable scientific hypothesis: The synergistic co-milling of a rigid carbon black (CB) scaffold with specific transition metals physically and chemically decouples the kinetic barriers of the AZ31 matrix. We postulate that the CB scaffold acts not merely as an additive, but as a rigid structural network that introduces a high density of interfacial defects (acting as "deep trap" nucleation sites) and physically anchors the microstructure.

Concurrently, the introduced transition metals (Ni or Ti) chemically lower local energy barriers and guide the microstructural evolution. If valid, this specific architecture should prevent the conventional high-temperature mechanistic shift toward agglomeration-driven bulk diffusion, thereby sustaining a rapid, dispersion-controlled interfacial transport.

Consequently, the core novelty of this work lies in elucidating a quantitative "mechanistic dichotomy" between a late-transition metal (Ni) and an early-transition metal (Ti) within an identical AZ31-CB platform, moving beyond empirical trial-and-error approaches. We hypothesize and subsequently demonstrate that Ni acts as a "kinetic pump," drastically lowering the surface activation barrier to drive ultra-fast hydrogen dissociation. Conversely, Ti functions primarily as a "structural anchor," exerting a profound Zener pinning effect that restricts high-temperature Mg grain coarsening, thereby preserving microstructural stability and ensuring high capacity utilization even at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 325 °C).

To rigorously test these hypotheses, this study synthesized AZ31-based composites modified with CB, Ni, and Ti through HEBM. The milling parameters were meticulously chosen based on prior studies [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ], which demonstrated their effectiveness in achieving optimal grain refinement while minimizing contamination. By varying the catalyst concentration (1 wt% vs. 2 wt%), we systematically analyze the impact of additive type on particle morphology and reaction mechanisms. To thoroughly assess the kinetic performance and thermodynamic stability, isothermal hydrogen absorption and desorption measurements were performed at 375, 350, and 325 °C. By deconvoluting the macroscopic kinetic parameters using the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) model and the Arrhenius equation—specifically analyzing the kinetic compensation effect—this study successfully distinguishes between surface-promoted kinetics and bulk diffusion-controlled mechanisms. Ultimately, this work provides new mechanistic insights into how strategically pairing a structural scaffold with targeted transition metals can reconcile ultra-fast reaction velocity with exceptional reversible storage capacity.

The key novelty of this study lies in the quantitative decoupling of the kinetic mechanisms across different temperatures. Unlike previous works that generally treat transition metals merely as surface catalysts, this study synergistically couples Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) modeling with pre-exponential factor (A) analysis to systematically distinguish the fundamentally different roles of Ni (a surface kinetic accelerator) and Ti (a bulk structural modifier). Furthermore, this dual-additive strategy (CB + Ni/Ti) effectively resolves the typical trade-off between structural agglomeration and chemical activation, offering a highly efficient route to achieve superior low-temperature hydrogen storage in commercial AZ31 alloys.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The primary materials used in this study were AZ31 magnesium alloy powder (purity > 99.9%, MACH Taiwan Co., Ltd.), carbon black (CB, purity > 99%, HOMYTECH Co., Ltd.), nickel powder (Ni, purity > 99.9%, EMPEROR CHEMICAL Co., Ltd.), and titanium powder (Ti, purity > 99.9%, Atomic Craft Corporation). The specific selection of Ni and Ti as additives was based on their distinct catalytic mechanisms: Ni (a late-transition metal) was chosen for its superior surface catalytic activity to accelerate hydrogen dissociation (targeting rapid kinetics), while Ti (an early-transition metal) was selected for its high thermal stability to exert a Zener pinning effect against high-temperature Mg grain coarsening (targeting microstructural stability).

sections.heading: Composite preparation
paragraphs: We made composite powders by using a high-energy ball mill (model: Retsch PM100). To ensure methodology clarity and prevent the oxidation of the highly reactive metallic surfaces, all material handling and the high-energy ball milling (HEBM) process were strictly conducted under a continuously purified argon atmosphere. The weight ratio of the balls to the powder was 30:1, and the milling speed was set to 300 rpm for three hours. To keep the machine from getting too hot, it had to stop for 10 min every 30 min of milling. These specific HEBM parameters were strategically adopted based on a highly optimized baseline established for the AZ31-Ni system in recent authoritative studies [ 7 ,  8 ] to ensure the optimal dispersion of the metallic phase while minimizing contamination.

Building upon this robust baseline, we isolated the effects of the additives by preparing a systematic series of samples. Specifically, the prepared composites included: pure AZ31, an AZ31 baseline milled with 3 wt% CB, and catalyzed AZ31 + 3CB composites modified with varying amounts of Ni (1 wt% and 2 wt%) or Ti (1 wt% and 2 wt%).

sections.heading: Characterization
paragraphs: The phase composition of the as-milled and hydrogenated powders was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a Bruker D2 PHASER X diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). To prevent surface oxidation and contamination, all powder samples were carefully loaded and sealed into a specialized airtight sample holder within an argon-filled glovebox (O2 and H 2 O < 0.1 ppm) prior to measurement. The diffraction patterns were recorded over a 2θ range of 20° to 80° with a scanning step of 0.05° and a scanning speed of 6°/min. The surface morphology and particle size distribution of the composite powders were examined using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, JEOL JSM-6390LV) operating at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Secondary electron (SE) imaging was utilized to capture the detailed surface topology of the composites. Simultaneously, to investigate the dispersion of the additives (Ni and Ti) within the AZ31 matrix, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping was performed in conjunction with the SEM observations. Additionally, the particle size distribution was quantitatively analyzed using a laser diffraction particle size analyzer (model: Beckman Coulter LS 230) located at National Taiwan University. The analyzer was calibrated using standard reference materials before testing, and each sample was measured three times to obtain a statistically significant average distribution. The operation details of some characterization items can refer to the literature (Water Research, 2025, 268: 122,627; Water Res., 2026, 288: 124,564; Water Research 2023, 244, 120,530; Water research 2023, 229, 119,456; Water Res., 2025, 287: 124,436)[ 10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 – 14 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogenation measurements
paragraphs: The hydrogen absorption and desorption properties of the composites were systematically evaluated using a Sieverts-type volumetric apparatus. For each measurement, approximately 0.3 g of the composite powder was loaded into the stainless steel reactor. Before the kinetic testing, an activation process was conducted at 375 °C, where the initial five absorption–desorption cycles were utilized to break down the surface oxide layer and stabilize the material's thermodynamic baseline. Specifically, each activation cycle consisted of a 2-h absorption period under 3.5 MPa of hydrogen, followed by a 1-h vacuum desorption at 0.08 MPa. After this activation period, data from the 6th to the 10th cycles recorded to evaluate the intrinsic hydrogenation kinetics and cycling stability. The measurements were taken at three different temperatures: 375, 350, and 325 °C. During each kinetic testing cycle, hydrogen absorption took place at a starting pressure of 3.5 MPa, and desorption took place at a vacuum pressure of 0.08 MPa. To ensure a robust and objective kinetic comparison across all temperatures, the macroscopic reaction time was strictly defined as the duration required to reach 95% of the maximum saturation capacity. This threshold effectively filters out the extreme uncertainties associated with the near-equilibrium asymptotic tail. Furthermore, a preliminary sensitivity analysis evaluating the completion times at 90% and 97% saturation confirmed that the relative kinetic rankings and comparative trends among all composites remain entirely consistent, validating the robustness of the chosen 95% threshold. The stabilized kinetic curves were subsequently utilized to perform Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) modeling and to extract the apparent activation energy (Ea) via the Arrhenius equation.

sections.heading: Phase composition and crystallite size
paragraphs: XRD was used to look at the phase compositions of the pure AZ31 and the AZ31-based composites that had been milled, as shown in Fig.  1 ; for all of the patterns, the main diffraction peaks were linked to the α-Mg solid solution phase (which is Mg 0.97 Zn 0.03 ). This phase is the main place where reversible hydrogen can be stored, and it sets the composite's theoretical capacity. Notably, there were no diffraction peaks for carbon black (CB), which is due to its amorphous nature. Even though XRD can't see it, CB is very important because it stops too much cold welding during milling, which makes it easier to make the particles smaller. Figure 1 XRD patterns of AZ31 and AZ31-based composites:  a  AZ31,  b  AZ31 + 3CB,  c  AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni,  d  AZ31 + 3CB + 2Ni,  e  AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti,  f  AZ31 + 3CB + 2Ti.

There were also no distinct peaks for the metallic additives (Ni, Ti) or any possible intermetallic compounds. However, this absence does not imply the lack of these catalytic species. Rather, it is fundamentally governed by the intrinsic instrumental limits of X-ray diffraction [ 15 ]. Specifically, the low doping concentration (1 to 2 wt%) falls inherently below the typical sensitivity threshold of conventional laboratory powder XRD (~ 3–5 wt%). Furthermore, the extreme nanoscale fragmentation induced by HEBM causes severe diffraction line broadening. Because the diffracted intensity is spread over a wider 2θ range, the faint signals of these trace additives merge completely into the background noise.

While direct atomic-scale visualization is absent, recent comprehensive studies on HEBM-processed Mg-based nanocomposites [ 16 ] explicitly confirm that ball milling effectively drives trace transition metal catalysts into a highly dispersed state over the newly formed host surfaces. This highly dispersed state maximizes the specific surface area for the hydrogen dissociation reaction (the spillover effect). Consequently, based on recent authoritative findings [ 17 ], we hypothesize that trace amounts of Ni on the Mg surface may react in situ upon hydrogen activation to form nanoscale Mg 2 Ni. This in situ-formed phase likely acts as an active catalytic gateway (the "hydrogen pump" effect) to facilitate rapid H 2  dissociation.

sections.heading: Microstructure and morphology
paragraphs: SEM was used to look at the surface morphology of the as-milled powders and how they changed after hydrogenation, as shown in Fig.  2 . In the as-milled state (top row), all samples showed a typical flake-like shape with wide, flat surfaces. This is what happens when you use high-energy ball milling to make plastic deform. But after the hydrogenation process (bottom row), the shape changed a lot and became finer, more granular particles. The volume changes that happen during the hydriding and dehydriding cycles cause the larger flakes to break down into smaller pieces. Figure 2 SEM micrographs showing the microstructural evolution of  a ,  e  pure AZ31,  b ,  f  AZ31 + 3CB,  c ,  g  AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni, and  d ,  h  AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti. Top row  a – d : as-milled powders; bottom row  e – h : after hydrogenation.

To further verify the presence and distribution of the metallic additives, which were not detected in the XRD patterns, SEM–EDS elemental mapping was performed on the AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni and AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti composites.

Figure  3  shows the results of elemental mapping for both the AZ31-1Ni and AZ31-1Ti composites. The bright spots in the mapping images show that the metallic additives are there and spread out. In both samples, the signals for the matrix elements (Mg, Al, Zn) and carbon (C) are evenly spread out. But the distribution of the metallic additives is very different. Figure  3 a shows that nickel (Ni) signals are evenly spread out across the matrix with no obvious separation. This means that the ball milling process worked well. Figure 3 SEM images and corresponding EDS elemental mapping of  a  AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni and  b  AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti composites.

Figure  3 b, on the other hand, shows that titanium (Ti) is not evenly spread out; instead, it is grouped together in certain areas, forming distinct agglomerates within the Mg matrix. To provide quantitative evidence for this microstructural observation, we analyzed the particle size distribution (PSD) in Table  2 , specifically focusing on the D 90  index which characterizes the coarse tail of the distribution. While the uniformly catalyzed Ni-sample maintains a D 90  of 234.30 μm, the Ti-doped composite exhibits an inherently massive D 90  of 318.00 μm. This extreme surge in the D 90  value (> 318 μm) serves as direct quantitative evidence that a substantial volume fraction of the Ti-doped powder has formed micro-scale agglomerates, perfectly aligning with the localized clusters visually observed in the EDS mapping (Fig.  3 ). Table 2 Particle size distribution parameters (D 10 , D 50 , D 90 ) of AZ31 and its composites Sample Average particle size (μm) D 10  (µm) D 50  (µm) D 90  (µm) AZ31 85.45 23.85 62.97 166.00 AZ31 + 3CB 97.42 37.08 89.45 171.30 AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni 129.50 36.39 96.55 234.30 AZ31 + 3CB + 2Ni 103.50 30.05 74.60 220.60 AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti 161.50 44.59 124.70 318.00 AZ31 + 3CB + 2Ti 152.90 41.29 123.10 310.10

Mechanistically, this structural constraint imposes a "double bottleneck" on the diffusion pathways. First, because of the severe agglomeration, the active catalytic gateways are restricted to isolated macroscopic "hotspots" rather than being uniformly distributed over the host surfaces. Second, because the overall host particles are significantly larger (D 50  = 124.70 μm), the dissociated hydrogen atoms must travel much longer distances through the Mg matrix to achieve full saturation. This combination physically mandates the overall rate-limiting step to shift from surface penetration toward long-range bulk diffusion, a transition that is quantitatively corroborated by the shift in the JMAK exponent discussed in Sect. " Desorption kinetics and activation energy ".

While the D 10  and D 90  values listed in Table  2  give us an idea of how wide the distribution is and how much agglomeration there is, but the median particle size D 50  was chosen as the main metric for comparison. The D 50  value is a better way to show the central tendency than the arithmetic mean because high-energy ball milling often leads to a wide and non-normal size distribution.

The particle size distribution, as shown in Fig.  4  and Table  2 , followed the order: AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti > AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni > AZ31 + 3CB > Pure AZ31. The average particle size of the Pure AZ31 sample was 62.97 µm, which was the smallest. The particle size grew to 89.45 µm when 3 wt% CB was added. Figure 4 Particle size (D 50 ) distributions for pure AZ31 and its composites.

Most notably, the Ti-containing composite exhibited the most significant particle coarsening. The AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti sample showed the largest average particle size of 124.70 µm, which is nearly double that of the pure AZ31. This quantitative result aligns perfectly with the SEM observations in Fig.  2 d, where we could clearly see a lot of agglomeration and big secondary particles. This occurrence is ascribed to the ductile characteristics of metallic titanium, which presumably enabled excessive cold welding during high-energy impact, surpassing the fracturing effect [ 18 ]. The sample with Ni (AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni) also showed a small increase in particle size to 96.55 µm compared to the sample with only CB. This suggests that metallic additives generally made particles stick together in this study [ 19 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogen storage performance
paragraphs: As shown in Fig.  5 , the composites exhibit a typical activation behavior during the initial cycles. The capacity fluctuates or gradually increases in the first few cycles (Cycles 1–5), which is attributed to the progressive breakdown of surface oxide layers and the creation of stable hydrogen diffusion pathways within the matrix. Following this activation period, the hydrogen storage capacity tends to stabilize, indicating that the system has reached a steady state. To guarantee the reliability of the kinetic analysis and to reduce experimental errors linked to the activation process, the kinetic parameters (including reaction rates and activation energy) presented in the following sections were obtained by averaging the data from the final five stabilized cycles (Cycles 6–10) (Fig.  6 ). Figure 5 Cyclic hydrogen storage performance of the composites at 375 °C:  a  absorption capacity,  b  desorption capacity, and  c  cycling stability. Figure 6 Hydrogen  a – c  absorption and  d – f  desorption curves of the AZ31 composites measured at different temperatures:  a ,  d  375 °C,  b ,  e  350 °C, and  c ,  f  325 °C.

Hydrogen storage properties were evaluated at 375, 350, and 325 °C. The reaction time was defined as the duration required to reach 95% of maximum saturation to exclude the slow diffusion tail. Notably, desorption at 325 °C did not reach equilibrium due to insufficient thermodynamic driving force; consequently, time was omitted for this condition, though total capacity is recorded in Table  3 . The kinetic data summarized in Table  3  and Fig.  7  show a clear order of performance based on the conditions in which they are used. The AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni composite had the fastest absorption kinetics, reaching 95% saturation in only 702 s at 375 °C. The AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti composite, on the other hand, worked very well at lower temperatures. It had the highest reversible capacity of 4.00 wt% even at the lowest operating temperature of 325 °C, which was much better than the other samples. To address the apparent contradiction between the massive particle coarsening of the Ti-doped composite (D 50  ≈ 124.7 µm) and its superior low-temperature capacity, it is essential to distinguish external geometry from internal microstructure. While macroscopic agglomeration reduces the external surface area, the addition of Ti fundamentally creates a massive network of internal "deep traps." At lower temperatures (e.g., 325 °C), un-catalyzed particles typically suffer from the kinetic "blocking effect," where an outer MgH 2  shell forms and prematurely halts further hydrogen penetration. However, the abundant Ti-induced internal defect pathways allow hydrogen to bypass this surface bottleneck, fully utilizing the bulk material. Furthermore, unlike Ni, Ti–rich interfaces can alter the local electronic structure, weakening adjacent Mg–H bonds and reducing the localized thermodynamic enthalpy penalty for phase transformation. Moreover, the detrimental effects of excessive loading are clear: Raising the additive content from 1 wt% to 2 wt% consistently reduced performance. For example, the Ti-series' capacity went from 4.00 wt% (1Ti) to 3.31 wt% (2Ti), and the reaction time got longer.

At 1 wt% loading, distinct kinetic mechanisms were observed. The Ni-containing composites exhibited the fastest kinetics, particularly at 375 °C. This acceleration is governed almost entirely by kinetic factors. Residing primarily at the surface, Ni facilitates a classic "hydrogen spillover effect," rapidly splitting H 2  molecules and drastically lowering the surface activation energy barrier. In contrast, the Ti-doped composite relies on the aforementioned synergistic combination of internal deep nucleation (structural kinetics) and localized thermodynamic softening to maximize capacity, albeit at the cost of a slower overall diffusion rate. Increasing the catalyst loading to 2 wt% universally resulted in decreased saturation capacity. This degradation is attributed to two factors: (1) the "dead weight" effect [ 20 ], where heavier transition metals reduce the weight fraction of the active Mg phase, and (2) severe particle agglomeration (as detailed in Sect. " Microstructure and morphology "), which diminishes the effective catalytic surface area. Consequently, 1 wt% was identified as the optimal concentration.

Table  4  benchmarks the hydrogen storage performance of the as-milled AZ31 composite against other Mg-based systems reported in recent literature [ 7 ,  8 ,  21 ]. To clearly highlight the superiority of the proposed synergistic modification, Table  4  benchmarks the kinetic performance of our composites against representative Mg-based systems at 375 °C. First, compared to AZ61-based alloys [ 21 ], the commercial AZ31 matrix inherently provides a higher theoretical hydrogen storage density due to its lower aluminum content (3 wt% vs. 6 wt%). However, un-catalyzed AZ31 suffers from sluggish kinetics. Our dual-additive strategy effectively resolves this bottleneck by decoupling structural and chemical barriers. When comparing our AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni composite to the AZ31 + 2Ni system reported in literature [ 8 ], a striking kinetic improvement is observed. While the system with 2 wt% Ni alone requires 2390 s to reach saturation absorption, our composite achieves 95% saturation in just 702 s—an over three-fold acceleration despite utilizing half the catalyst loading. This quantitatively demonstrates the crucial role of the CB scaffold: It prevents severe particle agglomeration during milling, thereby preserving an exceptionally high dispersion of the active Ni "hydrogen pump" sites.

Furthermore, when benchmarked against the AZ31 system modified solely with CB[ 7 ] (absorption time of 1244.8 s), the addition of just 1 wt% Ni drastically cuts the reaction time down to 702 s, verifying the indispensable surface spillover effect. Consequently, the AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni composite successfully bridges the gap between high gravimetric capacity and ultra-fast kinetics, proving the exceptional efficiency of coupling a rigid carbon network with a targeted transition metal.

sections.heading: Desorption kinetics and activation energy
paragraphs: To quantitatively elucidate the kinetic mechanisms governing the hydrogenation process and to rationalize the superior rate observed for the Ni-added composite, the absorption curves were analyzed using the JMAK model. Prior to the linear regression, the conversion fraction X(t) was strictly defined as X(t) = H(t) / H max , where H(t) is the absorbed capacity at time t and H max  is the maximum saturation capacity at the specific isothermal temperature. To isolate the steady-state nucleation and growth kinetics, the initial incubation period (t 0 , defined as the time required to reach X = 0.01) was explicitly excluded to filter out instrumental dead time and early-stage experimental noise. Consequently, the effective time t eff  = t–t 0  was utilized. To ensure statistical robustness and avoid non-linearities, the linear regression was strictly performed within the standardized fitting window of 0.2 ≤ X ≤ 0.8.The derived kinetic parameters, including the Avrami exponent (n) and the rate constant (k), along with their standard errors, are summarized in Table  5  and Fig.  8  JMAK analysis of hydrogen absorption kinetics: (a–c) reacted fraction (X) versus time and (d–f) corresponding JMAK plots at 375, 350, and 325 °C. To further interpret the transformation mechanism, the Avrami exponent (n) was analyzed based on classical JMAK kinetics, where n can be approximated as the sum of nucleation and growth contributions (n = a + bc), with a representing the nucleation behavior and bc related to the dimensionality of phase growth. In the present composites, the n values range from 1.05 to 1.83 (Table  5 ), suggesting that the hydrogenation process is governed by a combination of nucleation and diffusion-controlled growth mechanisms.

Considering the theoretical constraint that the nucleation index a varies between 0 (instantaneous nucleation) and 1 (continuous nucleation), the corresponding growth term (bc) is estimated to be close to ~ 1. This indicates that the growth process is likely dominated by low-dimensional vor interface-controlled diffusion, which is consistent with hydrogen transport along grain boundaries and defect-rich regions introduced by high-energy ball milling. Furthermore, the variation in n with temperature suggests a transition in nucleation behavior, where higher temperatures may promote more rapid activation of nucleation sites, leading to characteristics closer to instantaneous nucleation.

This choice is based on the fact that surface sensitivity can make the hydrogenation (absorption) process more complex. For example, native oxide layers or passivation films can create kinetic barriers that are not related to the material's intrinsic bulk properties. The breaking of Mg–H bonds and the formation of the Mg phase from the hydride matrix are what drive the dehydrogenation (desorption) process. So, the desorption kinetics give a more accurate and reliable measure of the energy barrier that needs to be crossed to break the bond stability. This makes it easier to judge how well the additives work as catalysts.

To quantitatively analyze the kinetic mechanisms and determine the energy barrier for hydrogen release, the desorption data measured at different temperatures were fitted using the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) model. It is noted that desorption kinetics were specifically selected for this analysis to minimize the experimental variables often associated with the absorption process (e.g., surface oxide barriers), thereby providing a more intrinsic evaluation of the Mg–H bond stability.

As a result, the hydrogenation reaction doesn't need an incubation period to make new nuclei. Instead, it happens quickly through the diffusion-driven growth of existing nuclei. This mechanism elucidates the rapid initial kinetics observed in the ball-milled composites relative to their unmilled counterparts [ 22 ].

Also, the intercept values (ln k) listed in Fig.  9  provide a direct comparison of the reaction rates. The AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ni sample exhibits the highest  k  value, consistent with its fastest desorption performance across all temperatures. In contrast, the kinetic analysis at 325 °C highlights a critical trade-off for the AZ31 + 3CB + 1Ti composite. But its lower rate constant (k) shows that the Ti agglomerates limit its speed. These rough particles make it harder for hydrogen atoms to move around, which slows down the reaction rate even though the storage capacity is high.

By plotting  ln k  versus  1000/T  as shown in Fig.  10 , the activation energy was derived from the slope of the fitted lines. The calculated kinetic parameters are summarized in Table  6 . Table  5  shows that raising the catalyst loading to 2 wt% did not lower the activation energy (Ea), which supports the strong agglomeration seen in Sect. " Microstructure and morphology ". So, the next part of the discussion will be about the intrinsic mechanisms of the optimized 1 wt% composites. Pure AZ31 had the lowest activation energy (139.1 kJ/mol), which goes against what is usually thought about catalysts. Adding catalysts made the apparent Ea values go up. The rise in Ea to 147.0 kJ/mol is due to the fact that carbon black (CB) acts as a dispersant. CB keeps a high density of lattice defects that ball milling adds by stopping sintering during processing. These defects are like deep hydrogen traps that need more thermal energy to be released, which raises the apparent activation energy. The addition of rigid additives (e.g., 3 wt% CB) slightly increases the apparent activation energy compared to pure AZ31. This elevation is physically attributed to the generation of defect-related deep hydrogen traps. To provide direct structural evidence for these traps, we evaluated the crystallite sizes via XRD peak broadening. Pure AZ31 exhibited a crystallite size of 17.68 nm. Remarkably, the synergistic addition of CB during high-energy ball milling drastically refined the crystallite size to 15.42 nm. As demonstrated by established literature on Mg-carbon composites [ 23 ], carbonaceous additives act as highly effective process control agents that prevent cold welding, driving severe nanoscale grain refinement. In classical trapping models, this massive proliferation of grain boundaries and Mg/C hetero-interfaces acts precisely as a network of deep physical traps. While escaping these defective boundaries requires slightly higher localized thermal energy (resulting in a higher apparent Ea), they simultaneously provide an abundance of active nucleation sites. This is quantitatively corroborated by the surge in the pre-exponential factor (A) from 1.8 × 10 8  (pure AZ31) to 3.4 × 10 8  (AZ31 + 3CB), mathematically confirming the structural–kinetic synergy of the defect-related traps. The activation energy for the nickel-containing composite was slightly lower than that for the CB-sample, at 141.3 kJ/mol. This means that the better kinetics seen in Sect. " Hydrogen storage performance " are not just because the energy barrier is lower. Instead, as previously discussed, Ni primarily resides at the surface and facilitates a classic "hydrogen spillover effect." Consistent with the "multistage hydrogen pump" mechanism [ 24 ], the in situ-formed Mg 2 Ni interfaces act as highly efficient kinetic gateways to rapidly dissociate H 2  molecules. Although the macroscopic Ea remains relatively high, these uniformly dispersed catalytic sites drastically lower the localized surface energy barrier, resulting in the fast initial reaction rates. The Ti-composite exhibited an activation energy of 182.0 kJ/mol, which presents an apparent kinetic paradox: It possesses a higher energy barrier but still achieves superior low-temperature capacity (as seen in Sect. " Hydrogen storage performance "). To quantitatively elucidate this contradiction, we evaluated the pre-exponential factor (A) derived from the intercept of the Arrhenius plot (Eq.  3 ). In solid–gas phase transformations, the A value is intrinsically proportional to the density of active heterogeneous nucleation sites. As calculated from our data, the addition of Ti leads to an exponential surge in the pre-exponential factor by nearly four orders of magnitude (A≈ 3.3 × 10 12 ), compared to pure AZ31 (A≈ 1.8 × 10 8 ). This massive proliferation of internal active sites quantitatively proves the generation of an extensive network of internal "deep traps" within the Ti-doped agglomerates. Therefore, while the higher Ea implies that individual atomic jumps require more thermal energy, the sheer overwhelming quantity of parallel reaction pathways (represented by the massive A factor) dominates the macroscopic sorption capacity. This synergy between structural defect density and thermodynamic pathways allows hydrogen to bypass the surface blocking effect and fully saturate the massive bulk of the Ti-doped composites at low temperatures.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Researchers looked closely at how well AZ31 composites with carbon black, nickel, and titanium could store hydrogen. Here are the main points of the conclusions. High-energy ball milling effectively reduced the AZ31 matrix grains to the nanoscale (~ 16 nm). There was, however, a clear difference in morphology: The Ni and CB additives kept the powder distribution fine, but the ductile titanium caused the particles to clump together (D 50  ≈ 124.7 µm), imposing a "double-bottleneck" effect on the subsequent kinetic mechanisms. Kinetic analysis showed that nickel speeds up the reaction by acting as a kinetic promoter (Ea ≈ 141.3 kJ/mol) and catalyzing it on the surface. In contrast, titanium changed the rate-limiting step toward long-range bulk lattice diffusion. This is shown by a much higher activation energy of 182.0 kJ/mol. However, this apparent kinetic limitation is overwhelmingly compensated by an exponential surge in the pre-exponential factor (A≈ 3.3 × 10 12 ). This indicates that Ti creates a massive network of internal "deep traps," allowing hydrogen to bypass surface blocking and fully saturate the bulk. The AZ31-1Ti composite had the highest reversible capacity of 4.00 wt% even though it worked at a low temperature of 325 °C. A catalyst loading of 1 wt% was found to be the best because higher concentrations caused agglomeration without any additional kinetic benefits. Because of this, Ti-based composites are better for applications that need a lot of capacity, while Ni-based composites are better for applications that need a fast rate.
